claims.text: The initial Mg-bearing lightweight HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with minimal large-scale precipitation or segregation.
Thermal exposure between approximately 400 and 700 °C drives precipitation from the metastable solid solution.
Local Mg supersaturation is the driving force for precipitation.
The thermally formed precipitates are Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Mg-rich intermetallic domains nucleate and grow both within the matrix and along grain boundaries.
Intermetallic precipitation produces local compositional changes and alters local chemical equilibria.
Intermetallic precipitation disrupts passivation mechanisms or passivation films.
Elevated-temperature diffusion of Mg out of the supersaturated solid solution produces the intermetallic phases.
Mg redistribution and intermetallic formation change the composition of the surface oxide.
The resulting surface changes reduce protective barriers and promote localized corrosion in saline media.
The resulting surface changes accelerate high-temperature oxidation and oxide-scale growth.
The as-synthesized alloy has moderate passivation and relatively high corrosion resistance.
The as-synthesized alloy has relatively high oxidation resistance.
Heat-treated samples will show distinctive Mg-rich precipitates relative to the initial state.
Heat-treated samples will have lower corrosion resistance in saline media than the initial state.
Heat-treated samples will exhibit faster oxide-scale growth than the initial state.
Below approximately 400 °C, diffusion-driven transformations are too slow to diminish corrosion or oxidation resistance.
Minor differences in alloy chemistry or processing can alter Mg diffusion rates, intermetallic compositions, precipitation onset temperature, and transformation kinetics.
